newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD reflects on role as it sheds Western label.
newsitem.headline: OECD reflects on role as it sheds Western label.

text.p: The OECD, once a cosy club of rich nations, met Tuesday to discuss its future role after recent expansion to embrace former Soviet bloc states such as the Czech Republic and Poland, but amid pressure to cut its costs.

Ministers from the 29 member states of the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development were also expected to sign a deal with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov forging closer ties, but keeping Russian membership at arm's length for the moment.

A draft of a statement the OECD planned to release after the signing pledges to "help the Russian Federation to meet and sustain all the conditions for membership of the OECD," but without setting a target date.

Donald Johnston, the Canadian Secretary General of the OECD, said in advance of the two-day annual OECD summit that Russian membership was the "shared goal" in the long term but that Moscow had a very long way to go on economic liberalisation before entry talks could even start.

The OECD's membership profile has changed dramatically in the past few years as it has opened its doors to less-wealthy countries like Mexico, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland and also spread its wings in Asia beyond Japan to include most recently South Korea.

Johnston said the enlargement of the OECD could prove to be a "thorny issue" at the summit, which gathers a mixture of finance, trade, social and foreign affairs ministers, noting that it came at a time when the OECD was already under severe budget pressures.

On the sidelines of the OECD meeting, European trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan met U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky to try to secure a deal cutting red tape in trade in pharmaceutical and other products between the European Union and the United States.

Despite a stalemate in Washington talks last week, Brittan hopes to clinch an agreement so that pharmaceutical, medical and other products certified in the European Union would not need double-checking in the United States and vice-versa.

Brittan put a proposal to Barshefsky in a morning meeting, was expecting a second meeting later, and was clinging to hopes a deal could be struck before Clinton meets European Commission President Jacques Santer on Wednesday.

EU officials said there was agreement on the so-called mutual recognition mechanism as far as telecommunications products, such as telephones and computers, were concerned and also on small electrical equipment, such as kitchen appliances.

The trouble spots were pharmaceutical products and medical devices. An agreement across all sectors would concern trade in products worth an estimated $40 billion, according to U.S. estimates, one of the EU officials said.
